reconcile.connective: Keil and Delitzsch name the crux directly, resolving it: commended mirth is enjoyment conditioned by the fear of God, not unconditional pleasure.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible sets Proverbs 17:22 and Ecclesiastes 8:15 flatly against Ecclesiastes 7:3-4 and Luke 6:25 as opposite verdicts on mirth.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/happy.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: How this saying agrees with Koheleth's ultimatum: There is nothing better than to eat and drink, etc. (Ecc 2:24, etc.), the Talmudists have been utterly perplexed to discover; Manasse ben-Israel in his Conciliador (1632) loses himself in much useless discussion. … The solution of the difficulty is easy. The ultimatum does not relate to an unconditional enjoyment of life, but to an enjoyment conditioned by the fear of God.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: K&D explicitly name the crux (Eccl 7's preference for the house of mourning over mirth vs. Qohelet's recurring 'eat, drink, be merry' ultimatum, the same formula behind 8:15) and resolve it by qualifying the commended enjoyment as fear-of-God-conditioned, not unconditional indulgence.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley's 'Laughter' entry lines up Proverbs 17:22 and Ecclesiastes 8:15 (commended) against Ecclesiastes 7:3-4 and Luke 6:25 (condemned) — the same verse set as this contradiction — and resolves it: 'Not laughter in the abstract, but laughter under certain circumstances, is condemned.'

link.title: Defending Inerrancy: Ecclesiastes 2:2 — Is laughter good or bad?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment citing Prov 17:22, Eccl 7:3, Eccl 8:15, and Luke 6:25 together; resolves via Ecclesiastes 3:1,4 ('a time to laugh ... a time to mourn').
